body_text:
Last Call

Nina inherits The Last Call, her late uncle's failing dive bar — and the debt he owed to the man who really owns the block. The bartender came with the building and knows where every body is buried. A regular with money keeps tipping like he's buying something. The cook runs the kitchen like it's hers. The supplier sets his own terms. And every week, the collector knocks. Keep the lights on, or lose the only thing she's got left.

We're a small indie studio crafting intimate, story-driven experiences. Every game is made with care, and your support helps us keep creating. If you enjoy our work, consider supporting us!

body_text:
Canvas: First night (canvas_first_night) | Node: First night



Sully's keyring: a worn bottle opener and a tag that says NOT THE GOOD WHISKEY in his hand. The lock sticks, like he always said. You let yourself in.

The lights are behind the register. The Last Call comes up around you — cracked booths, the dead letter in the beer sign, a jukebox in the corner. It's yours now.

A man is wiping down the taps like he never stopped. Big, grey, a towel on his shoulder. He doesn't startle when the lights come on. He just looks at you the way you'd look at weather you'd been expecting.

You'd be Sully's niece. He talked about you. I'm Sal — I pour, I lock up, I been doing both since before you could see over the bar.

Ask about the envelope by the register.

body_text:
Canvas: The Last Call — Sal (canvas_sal_ropes_first) | Node: Working the bar



Sal slides down to make room and starts talking — which tap runs foam, which regular runs a tab, where Sully kept the good stuff. You keep up. You've poured in worse rooms than this.

By the second rush he stops narrating and just works beside you.

Huh. You've done this. Sully said you tended in the city. I figured he was bragging.

💭 You are thinking: First thing today that felt like solid ground.







Let him show you how Sully ran the place.

body_text:
Canvas: Sal — after the lock turns (canvas_sal_afterhours_hub) | Node: After close




Last customer's gone, the bolt's thrown, the neon's off. Sal counts the till by the register light and doesn't tell you to go home — but he doesn't look up either. You're Sully's niece who can pour. The quiet's just quiet.









Not yet — he locks up beside me and says goodnight, and I haven't given him a reason to want more.
Head up, call it a night.

body_text:
Canvas: Sal — the night he stays (canvas_sal_after_hours) | Node: After the lock turns



He's wiping down the well when he stops, both hands flat on the bar, and looks at you across it the way he's been not-looking at you for weeks. The register light buzzes. Somewhere a cooler kicks on. He doesn't say the thing — Sal never says the thing — he just comes around to your side of the bar, slow enough that you could step back if you wanted to, and you don't.

His hand finds the side of your jaw, rough from thirty years of work, careful like he's handling something he can't afford to drop. He smells like beer and bar soap and the cold off the cellar stairs. When he kisses you it's nothing like you braced for — not hungry, not taking, just sure, the way he does everything behind this bar he's run longer than you've been alive.

💭 You are thinking: Every man in my life has wanted something from me since I got off that bus. He's the first one who waited until I wanted it too.

...Lock's already thrown. Stay a while. I'll kill the lights.








Stay. Let the rest of the world wait outside the bolt.
Kiss him back, then make him say goodnight — not yet, not all of it.
